useCases.title: Hologram: a browser for decentralized AI chatbot services, self-hosted and verified before the first message
useCases.summary: Hologram Messaging turns the messenger into a browser for decentralized services: scan a QR and you are in an encrypted DIDComm chat with a self-hosted chatbot or AI agent, verified before the first message. It is built on Verana, the open public trust layer: every service is a Verifiable Service whose identity, operator and permissions any wallet can resolve. Five production services show the range: an Avatar credential issuer, a Passport issuer with NFC and liveness, AI agents for GitHub and Wise over MCP gated by your Avatar credential, and an X agent whose right to post is bound to verifiable credentials. Everything is open source and self-hosted from forkable repos: no app store, no platform, no vendor lock-in.
useCases.userJourney: Hologram Messaging is an open-source messenger that doubles as a browser: scanning a QR opens an encrypted DIDComm chat with a self-hosted service. No app store, no platform account. Each demo runs from a forkable repo (GitHub Actions deploy to Kubernetes) behind an open-source Verana VS Agent. A self-hosted organization anchor obtains Organization and Service credentials, runs its own trust registry on the Verana Verifiable Public Registry, and accredits its child services, so the app can trust-resolve every service before the first message. The Avatar chatbot issues you an identity credential in conversation; the Passport issuer reads a government ID over NFC and verifies liveness on a video call. The GitHub and Wise agents are AI assistants over MCP: they authenticate you with your Avatar credential, then act on your own accounts with your own API token, inside the encrypted chat. The X Agent flips authority around: an Agent Pack policy binds the right to post in the account's name to verifiable credentials you choose, so every AI action is credential-gated and attributable.

useCases.title: Mobile Driving Licence (mDL) based on ISO/IEC 18013-5
useCases.summary:
The mobile driving licence (mDL) is a digital version of a physical licence, held in a secure wallet on a smartphone. Built on ISO/IEC 18013-5, it enables trusted, privacy-preserving verification of licence data in person and, via ISO/IEC 18013-7, online. Selective disclosure lets holders share only requested data, while signatures, device binding, and holder authentication ensure the data is authentic and unaltered.

Since 2014, experts have collaborated through 100+ ISO meetings on a generic, interoperable model for verifiable credentials, initially focused on mDLs. In 2018, AAMVA, eReg, and Austroads formalised cooperation in their first global summit. Stakeholders collaborate further in test events (15 held). ISO/IEC 18013-5 was published in 2021, and Part 7 in 2024. The mdoc model supports many credential types, with growing adoption of Photo IDs.

This work has driven policy adoption, including the US REAL ID Modernization Act, the DHS mDL Rule, implementing acts for the EUDI Wallet, and more. Millions of ISO-compliant mDLs are provisioned across 23 AAMVA jurisdictions, next to mdoc deployments in Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Philippines, India, Argentina and the EU.
useCases.userJourney:
ISO/IEC 18013-5 defines three roles: an Issuer, a Holder's Wallet on a mobile device, and a Reader run by a Relying Party. The Issuer provisions the mDL into the Wallet using a standardised doctype and namespaces. To present it, the Holder opens the Wallet and connects to the Reader via QR code or NFC tap, then exchanges data over Bluetooth, Wi-Fi Aware or NFC. The Reader requests data elements; the Holder consents, and the Wallet returns only approved data, signed and bound to the device. This enables secure, selective, privacy-preserving offline verification of transaction data. ISO/IEC 18013-7 adds a remote, online mechanism. Since the mdoc model is generic, the same architecture extends to other credentials, such as Photo IDs.

Interoperability test events were at the core of collaboration to internationally recognise mDLs. Since 2018, AAMVA, eReg and Austroads have endorsed test events that brought issuers, wallets and readers together, pairing real implementations from different countries and vendors device to device to run engagement, data exchange and verification live, identifying gaps and maturing the global mDL ecosystem.

useCases.title: Cryptographically Verifiable Digital Product Passports for EU Battery Regulation Compliance
useCases.summary:
European manufacturers must issue Digital Product Passports (EU Battery Regulation
2023/1542, from 18 February 2027, with the ESPR extending this to further
categories). Today the data those passports need lives in unstructured PDF
datasheets, and manufacturers have no way to prove a downstream party has not
altered the file after publication.

AAS Studio turns a datasheet into a conformant Asset Administration Shell (IDTA,
IEC 63278-1:2023), then issues a W3C Verifiable Credential (VCDM 2.0, JWT-VC, and
an SD-JWT-VC variant with selective disclosure) committing to a canonical hash of
the passport content. The manufacturer is the issuer, signing with a tenant-scoped
ES256 key. Any verifier — regulator, recycler, supply-chain partner — checks the
credential against a public JWKS with no account and no call back to AAS Studio:
verification is fully offline. Revocation is enforced via a Bitstring/Token Status
List.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Manufacturer uploads a PDF datasheet; AAS Studio extracts the regulatory fields
   with an LLM ensemble and maps them onto a conformant Asset Administration Shell,
   validated against the official IDTA test engine.
2. AAS Studio computes a canonical hash of the passport content and issues a W3C
   Verifiable Credential signed with the manufacturer's own ES256 key, optionally
   as an SD-JWT-VC for selective disclosure.
3. If issued as revocable, a Bitstring/Token Status List slot is allocated; the
   manufacturer can revoke it later, effective immediately for any verifier.
4. The holder presents the credential's JWT to a relying party by any channel.
5. The relying party verifies it fully offline: it fetches the public JWKS and
   re-derives the proof itself, including the status-list check, so the verdict
   never depends on trusting AAS Studio's server.

useCases.title: Aptitude verifier for DTC-VC in PhotoID format - Supporting various experimentations for digital border crossing
useCases.summary:
Within the European APTITUDE Large Scale Pilot, a dedicated verifier for border crossing demonstrates how a government-backed digital service can collect and verify a Digital Travel Credential - Virtual Component. The credential is derived from any passport and securely stored within a digital identity wallet (i.e. France Identité), its format is based ISO/IEC standard and can be shared for verification in proximity at border crossing.
Multiple experimentations are and will be taking place over the next few months within APTITUDE consortium across the globe to support and enhance border crossings: Marseille Provence Airport, Coquelles Eurotunnel, Roissy Charles de Gaulle, Spain, Frankfurt, Helsinki, London, Hong-Kong.
The verifier serves travelers, border authorities, government agencies but also airports and airlines by enabling trusted, privacy-preserving identity verification using selective disclosure when needed. Through interoperability testing and real-world airport experiments, the solution demonstrates seamless credential exchange across multiple passport' nationalities, issuers, and verifiers from different countries.

useCases.title: Seal: independent review of AI decision evidence
useCases.summary: A bank declines a loan application. Six months later, the customer's solicitor asks why. The only record is a log written by the organisation under review. Seal separates the evidence across three independent parties: Seal signs the decision receipt, Yivi issues the reviewer's credential, and the reviewer signs the verdict. No single party controls the complete evidence path. A reviewer opens a docket with one fixed question, set before the evidence is opened so it cannot be adjusted to fit the answer, verifies the receipt against Seal's published key, and records one of three verdicts: accepted, declined, or not enough to answer. A reviewer outside Aqta, holding a credential we did not issue, has completed the prototype flow and signed a verdict. Walk it at review.aqta.ai or tamper with a receipt at app.aqta.ai/demo. What it establishes: Seal signed the stated record; signed fields have not changed; a reviewer signed a verdict on a fixed question. What it does not establish: that the record matches the computation that ran, or that every decision was recorded. We would rather be checked than believed. Signing is production; this review flow is a prototype and the page says so.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Seal signs an AI decision as it is made. The receipt is offline-verifiable against Seal's published Ed25519 key
2. A reviewer opens a docket: one fixed question, set before the evidence is opened so it cannot be adjusted to fit the answer, with the receipt attached. The question is hashed into what will be signed
3. The reviewer verifies the receipt in their own browser against the published key, then chooses one of three verdicts: accept, decline, or not enough to answer
4. The page requests an IRMA signature session. The reviewer's Yivi wallet shows the exact binding text: receipt hash, question hash, decision, timestamp
5. The reviewer signs by disclosing a verified email credential from their wallet. No account is created with the relying party
6. The relying party verifies that attribute-based signature with irmago, the open-source IRMA library, the moment anchored by the Yivi timestamp service
7. The pack exports receipt, credential presentation and countersignature. Each verifies without contacting Aqta: the receipt with the open-source verifiers on npm and PyPI, the signature with irmago, since no browser Idemix verifier exists

useCases.title: Establish a New Company in One Day — Company Passport
useCases.summary:
Starting a company in the Netherlands takes about six weeks: a notary draws up the deed, KVK registers the company, the Belastingdienst issues a VAT number, and only then can a bank open a business account. Each step waits on paper from the last. Supplier onboarding is just as document-heavy: KVK extracts, tax statements, insurance and IBAN details exchanged as PDFs over email.

The Company Passport initiative — a Dutch public-private partnership of KVK, Belastingdienst, KNB (notaries), NVB and Betaalvereniging Nederland — replaces these documents with verifiable credentials issued directly by authoritative sources. Credenco delivers the sandbox, the eIDAS 2.0 / DIIP v5-compliant Business Wallet and the Issuer Portals that power the initiative.

Each authority reads the credential issued by the previous one and completes its step the same day: incorporation drops from six weeks to one day, supplier onboarding from weeks to minutes, and falsified documents become technically impossible.
useCases.userJourney:
1. The notary drafts the deed of incorporation, signs it cryptographically and issues it as a verifiable credential into the company's Credenco Business Wallet (OpenID4VCI).

2. KVK reads the deed credential, registers the company the same day and issues the KVK Registration Extract (incl. LPID and UBO data) as a credential.

3. The Belastingdienst reads the KVK extract and issues the VAT number / tax compliance credential.

4. The bank reads all three credentials, opens the business account and issues an IBAN attestation.

5. From then on, supplier onboarding is trivial: a procurement platform requests KVK, tax, VAT, IBAN and insurance credentials in a single flow (OpenID4VP). The supplier shares them in one tap from the Business Wallet, and the platform verifies the issuers' signatures in real time.

6. Result: one source document, multiple readers, instant trust — six weeks becomes one day, and onboarding checks run without PDFs, email or manual review.

useCases.title: Direct e-Invoicing Small Scale Pilot
useCases.summary:
Invoice fraud, IBAN manipulation and mismatched VAT numbers cost European businesses billions every year. Today's e-invoicing is only half-digital: invoices move as PDFs or XML, but the sender's identity is never cryptographically proven.

The e-Invoicing pilot coordinated by FIDES Labs — with KVK, the Belastingdienst, Unifiedpost and Visma Yuki — was delivered as three projects. In projects 1 and 3, Credenco and Sphereon worked side by side, each with their own Business Wallet, proving true cross-vendor interoperability. Project 2, the FIDES Blue Pages — a decentralised catalogue of verifiable business identity — was delivered by Credenco.

KVK and the Belastingdienst issue company credentials into the wallets, and every invoice travels wallet-to-wallet as an e-Invoice credential, cryptographically bound to the sender's KVK, VAT and IBAN. Receivers validate all three in a single check against EBSI — invoices enter the ERP pre-verified.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Onboarding — KVK issues the Chamber of Commerce number and RSIN, the Belastingdienst the VAT number and tax address, as verifiable credentials into each company's Credenco Business Wallet (OpenID4VCI). All parties are registered on the EBSI trust registry.

2. Sending — from the supplier's ERP, the invoice is passed to the Business Wallet, which wraps it in an e-Invoice credential: signed and linked to the sender's KVK, VAT and IBAN credentials, with optional evidence documents.

3. Transport — the Send Invoice API delivers the credential straight into the receiver's wallet inbox; OpenID4VP authorises the transfer. No shared mailboxes, no attachments.

4. Receiving — the receiver's wallet verifies sender identity, VAT number and IBAN against trusted issuers on EBSI. The invoice enters the ERP pre-verified, ready for straight-through processing.

5. Discovery — via FIDES Blue Pages (delivered by Credenco as project 2), organisations look up verifiable counterparty data, read from each entity's DID. In projects 1 and 3, Credenco and Sphereon Business Wallets exchanged credentials interoperably.

useCases.title: Decentralized PHC Credentials in the Future AI Era.
useCases.summary:
The primary motivation behind creating this proof of concept is to demonstrate how Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) and Verifiable Credentials (VCs), aligned with W3C standards, can be integrated with on-chain blockchain technology i.e (CHEQD). This approach enables the deployment, storage, and verification of proof of human identity.
What it does
1.Government ID Issuance: A government agency issues an ID to the holder, which is required to obtain a PHC Verifiable Credential (VC).

2.Presenting ID to PHC Provider: The holder presents their government-issued VC from their wallet to the PHC provider, a trusted authority.

3.Fingerprint Biometric Capture: Once the government ID is verified, the user scans their fingerprint using PHC’s biometric infrastructure, which extracts unique fingerprint features.

4.Online Authentication : When accessing an online service that requires PHC verification, the user shares the PHC credential from their wallet with the service.

5.Verification Process: The service provider’s DIDComm v2 agent performs ZKP verification with the holder’s data. If verified, access is granted; otherwise, it is denied.
useCases.userJourney:
The DIDComm v2 agent is implemented entirely in Python, enabling secure message exchange between the Issuer, Holder, and Verifier.
DID:Peer protocol implementation and DID generation are also developed in Python.
We use the Universal DID Resolver/Registrar with cheqd to register and resolve DIDs on the cheqd testnet.
The complete Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) circuit is written in Circom, with proofs generated using the Circom compiler.

Proof Generation Flow

Feature Extraction: Fingerprint bifurcation and termination points are extracted, flattened, and combined into a single array.

Poseidon Merkle Tree: The data is hashed into a Poseidon-based Merkle tree, producing the root commitment and 8 sibling hashes for efficient proof generation.

Proof Generation: The Circom circuit compiles using these hashes to generate the proof, verification key, and public inputs, which are signed by the issuer.

Verification: The verifier extracts the proof and public inputs from the credential and validates them using zk-SNARKs, returning true or false.

useCases.title: Trusted Caller Identity
useCases.summary:
Call centre authentication still relies on security questions and SMS OTPs, which can be stolen, spoofed or defeated by SIM swap. Customers must disclose personal data to agents who have no need to see it.

Trusted Caller Identity replaces this with a verifiable credential. Telefónica issues a credential proving phone number ownership, secured by its Number Verify and SIM Swap network APIs. When a customer calls, the contact centre opens an encrypted DIDComm channel to their wallet and the customer confirms biometrically on their own device. Selective disclosure returns only a yes/no answer, so no personal data reaches the agent. Verification time reduces >4 times.

Four organisations across telecoms, identity and standards built it: Telefónica Tech (issuer, network signals), Dock Labs/Truvera (credential infrastructure), TMT ID (identity data), GSMA (coordination). The customer holds the credential, the contact centre verifies it, and no party sits in the middle.

It uses open verifiable credential and DIDComm standards, and Telefónica's network APIs sit within GSMA Open Gateway, so the model can scale to any operator rather than stay proprietary. Demonstrated at M
useCases.userJourney:
Setup, once
1. Telefónica verifies the customer's number and device via its Number Verify and SIM Swap APIs, confirming control of the number and that no recent SIM change occurred.
2. It issues a verifiable credential proving phone number ownership.
3. The credential is delivered to the customer's wallet and stored on device, not in a central database. In production the wallet will sit inside the operator's existing app.

On the call
4. The customer calls; the agent or IVR triggers authentication.
5. The contact centre, as verifier, sends an encrypted DIDComm request straight to the customer's wallet.
6. The customer gets a push notification and approves biometrically on their own device. The biometric never leaves the phone.
7. The wallet returns a cryptographic proof. Selective disclosure means only a yes/no reaches the agent, no personal data.
8. The contact centre verifies against Telefónica's issuer key without contacting the operator, so the operator learns nothing about where the customer authenticates. Done in 15-20 seconds.

useCases.title: DPPskop – Digital Product Passport Platform for ESPR Compliance

useCases.title: Company Compass

For many entrepreneurs, setting up a legal entity is a complex and time-consuming process due to the involvement of various bodies, such as the notary, the Chamber of Commerce, the tax authorities, banks and wallet providers. Due to the various routes, the fragmentation of systems and the lack of overview, business owners often lose track of things, make mistakes or experience unnecessary delays. 

The Company Compass process guidance application can solve this problem by acting as a central guide that provides step-by-step guidance, validates data, automatically synchronises with various parties and thus minimises errors. This leads to greater efficiency, shorter lead times and a smooth start to the business.

The process guidance application was created within Company Passport, a public-private collaboration of KNB, KVK, Belastingdienst, NVB and Betaalvereniging Nederland. The application exists as a functional demo.
useCases.userJourney: To establish a business in his/her name, the user needs a personal wallet in which his/het verified identity is recorded. The wallet is then linked to Company Compass. This ensures a safe and efficient way to identify the user when retrieving business data. The app then guides the user through all steps necessary to create a private limited company (BV). The application never stores data; the required data is always retrieved from the users digital wallet(s).

useCases.title: inGo - Digital, Verifiable and Secure Subcontractor Management Including Physical Access
useCases.summary:
Checking documents, monitoring deadlines, and granting site access for subcontractors is still often handled manually, with paper folders and spreadsheets - on construction sites, in logistics, and in technical services alike.
inGo digitalizes this process using decentralized identities (DIDs), digital wallets, and Verifiable Credentials (VCs), built on open standards (OpenID4VCI/VP, EUDI Wallet ARF) so it interoperates with other EUDI-ARF-conformant wallets rather than locking participants into a single vendor.
Employees receive credentials - such as site certificates, ID cards, work permits, or safety training - directly in their personal wallet. Using selective disclosure (SD-JWT VC), they can prove only what's required for a check, e.g. a valid access permit, without revealing unrelated personal data.
General contractors gain a real-time, cryptographically verifiable overview of credentials, deadlines, and site access. Subcontractors manage documents and credentials for their employees once and reuse them across projects - replacing manual paper checks with instant, auditable verification, on a secure, privacy-preserving, GDPR-compliant foundation.

issuers.labelRaw: General contractors and subcontractors (issuing site and access credentials); external trusted issuers such as government authorities, insurance companies, or certification bodies (planned)

credentials.labelRaw: Site Certificate, ID Card, Work Allowance, Visa, Social Security, Minimum Wage. The inGo system allows additional credential types like Safety Training and many more.

rps.labelRaw: General contractors / site management, access control systems (turnstiles), authorities/customs during inspections

useCases.userJourney:
inGo enables a range of processes built on wallets and Verifiable Credentials: 
1.	Onboarding: General contractors and subcontractors set up business wallets to manage employees and share project access.
2.	Issuance: Subcontractors and general contractors issue credentials (site certificates, ID cards, work permits, safety training) as Verifiable Credentials into each employee's personal wallet.
3.	Verification: The credentials are used to gain a verified site access, at site entrances (e.g. turnstiles) or during inspections inGo can tell if all required documents are available and valid in seconds - no paper, no manual lookup.
4.	Selective disclosure: Employees share only the specific attribute needed (e.g. "valid access permit: yes"), not full documents.
5.	Audit trail: Every verification is logged in an auditable, GDPR-compliant record.
External trusted issuers - e.g. government authorities, insurance companies, or certification bodies - are planned as additional issuers (e.g. state-verified identity, insurance proof).

useCases.title: Age verification as a service: wallet-native "over 18" for any platform, via an intermediary layer
useCases.summary:
Online platforms must verify users are over 18 to comply with DSA Article 28 and national law — but the traditional route forces users to expose their identity to prove a single fact, and building a wallet-native verifier in-house is out of reach for most businesses.

espuni is an independent intermediary layer that provides age verification as a service on top of EUDIPLO (OWF). Instead of each platform building and maintaining its own EUDI verifier, any service integrates once and lets espuni handle the wallet interaction, the trust-list validation, and the protocol complexity.

The user presents a proof-of-age credential from their EUDI Wallet; espuni requests only the "over 18" attribute, validates the issuer against the EU Age Verification Trusted List, and returns a yes/no. No name, no birthdate, no document reaches the platform.
Built on open standards (OID4VP, ISO 18013-7) and open source, it supports the Digital Credentials API with QR fallback, and works across EUDI wallets. The intermediary model is what makes wallet-native age verification realistic for the small and mid-sized businesses that can't build it themselves — a practical on-ramp to the EUDI ecosystem.
useCases.userJourney:
1 - A platform with an age-verification obligation (a shop, a streaming service, a gambling operator) integrates espuni once — a single integration instead of building an EUDI verifier from scratch.
2 - A user reaches age-restricted content. Instead of uploading a document, they're offered "Verify with your EUDI Wallet."
3 - espuni sends a presentation request for the age_over_18 attribute only — via the Digital Credentials API by default, but falling back to QR code if DC API is not available or rejected by the user.
4 - The user's EUDI Wallet shows exactly what's being requested — only "over 18," nothing else — and the user approves.
espuni receives the response, validates the issuer against the EU Age Verification Trusted List, and verifies the proof.
5 - The platform receives a verified yes/no. It never sees the user's identity, and the wallet interaction, trust validation, and protocol handling all happened in the intermediary layer — invisible to both the platform and the user.

The platform gets compliance without building or maintaining identity infrastructure; the user proves age without exposing identity; the exchange leaves an auditable cryptographic record.

useCases.title: DIFO - Digital Invoice Financing Origination for SMEs (Serbia & Romania pilot)
useCases.summary: DIFO is an open-source protocol, developed in partnership with Finspot, IFC, World Bank, GLEIF and Global vLEI AB. It uses zero-knowledge proofs, verifiable credentials vLEI and other tech to make invoice due diligence independently verifiable - assess once, verifiable by all. Any investor can then verify the integrity and provenance of due diligence data, without dependency on specific platforms. It eliminates repeated identity and data verifications, shifting trust from the channel to the underlying source. It makes access to finance for small-ticket invoices more economical, extending supply of working capital to SMEs. Originators produce cryptographic proofs of origination facts  such as seller identity, buyer acceptance, sanctions, fraud prevention, and legal notice; raw documents never leave their systems. Proofs are anchored on-chain and issued as W3C VerCreds / KERI ACDC, with vLEI credentials anchoring organizational trust. A completed pilot verified 58 invoices from 24 SMEs across Serbia and Romania, issuing 200+ verifiable proofs; an international debt fund confirmed DIFO-verified portfolios merit a distinct asset class. Verification costs fall below $2 per invoice;

issuers.labelRaw: Licensed issuers of Republic of Serbia

credentials.labelRaw: EIDAS qualified certificate for electronic signature

rps.labelRaw: Advanced Global Capital Debt Fund\Pilot observer

useCases.userJourney: An SME requests early payment on an invoice from a licensed factoring originator (Finspot in Serbia, InvoiceCash in Romania). The originator uploads the invoice and its evidence to the DIFO instance: the qualified-signed invoice, the buyer's acceptance (signed national e-invoicing response or signed confirmation PDF), and the debtor notification email. DIFO then collects signed attestations from ecosystem issuers - a TSA-anchored AML screening response and a double-financing registry response signed with the Serbian Chamber of Commerce's vLEI via Global vLei wallet. For each of five facts (seller identity, buyer acceptance, sanctions, double financing, legal notice), a parser extracts properties at the originator's edge and a zero-knowledge prover generates a proof - raw data never leaves the originator. Proofs are verified on-chain and issued as W3C Verifiable Credentials / KERI ACDC, held in the originator's business wallet. A funder (AGC Capital in the pilot) verifies the credentials independently against public verifier contracts - no repeated due diligence, no raw documents. Verified invoices from multiple originators can then be pooled into one fundable portfolio.

useCases.title: One EUDI Wallet Release Across OpenID Foundation, WE BUILD and FCAF
useCases.summary:
Before releasing a new EUDI Wallet build, a wallet development team must show that the same app can receive and present credentials correctly across independent test ecosystems. Today this often requires separate manual sessions, provider-specific scripts and test code added to the application.

In the implemented Credimi workflow, a release candidate running on a real Android device is tested against OpenID Foundation and WE BUILD services. The wallet receives a test credential through OpenID4VCI and presents a PID-format SD-JWT VC through OpenID4VP. Credimi automates the wallet actions and API interactions, captures structured results, screenshots, video and device logs, and extracts the applicable FCAF test results from that evidence.

The developer can identify the failed requirement, fix the wallet and rerun exactly the same journey. Keeping the test logic outside the application substantially reduces implementation effort. The automation pipelines, adapters and evidence definitions can be reused across wallet releases and implementations, turning separate ecosystem tests into a shared and repeatable release-validation process.
useCases.userJourney:
Credimi makes external interoperability and conformance services easy to integrate into the same wallet-testing workflow, including OpenID Foundation and WE BUILD tests.

1. The developer configures their Wallet component in credimi.io.
2. They adapt Credimi’s published Maestro mobile-automation scripts to their wallet. Typically, 80–90% of each script can be reused, so the tests remain outside the wallet application rather than requiring test-specific code in it.
3. The developer launches a pipeline on a Credimi Runner. The runner executes the automation on a physical device, emulator or simulator and extracts the applicable FCAF test results from the pipeline evidence.
4. After execution, Credimi presents a detailed report showing every FCAF test performed, its result and the supporting execution evidence. The developer can inspect failures, adapt the wallet or script, and rerun the same pipeline.
5. Pipelines can also run automatically on a schedule or through CI integration, allowing the same reusable tests to validate subsequent wallet releases.

useCases.title: Municipal login with attribute-based credentials
useCases.summary: Citizens log in to their municipal account and securely share only the personal attributes a service actually needs, using an attribute-based wallet. The municipality acts as the relying party and verifies the presented attributes over the IRMA protocol. This is one of the first production implementations of attribute-based authentication in Dutch municipal services, showing that privacy-friendly login at scale is possible today.
useCases.userJourney:
1) The citizen has loaded personal attributes (e.g. name, email, mobile number) into an attribute-based wallet.
2) They open their municipal account and choose to log in with the wallet.
3) The municipality (relying party) requests only the attributes required for the service over the IRMA protocol.
4) The citizen reviews the request in the wallet and confirms disclosure.
5) The municipality verifies the attributes and grants access, without storing more personal data than necessary.

useCases.title: Enabling Digital Trust for Cross-Border Factoring of Used Cars and Auto Parts
useCases.summary:
TOPPAN and SBI XDC Network APAC are collaborating on a factoring solution for cross-border export transactions, verifiable corporate identity with blockchain-based financing. TOPPAN is Japan’s first qualified vLEI issuer. The vLEI is a digital credential based on the Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) system and enables trusted digital verification of a legal entity and its authorized representatives. The Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation (GLEIF), a not-for-profit organization that oversees the global LEI system, provides the framework for standardized legal-entity identification and verification. SBI XDC Network APAC, a joint venture between SBI Holdings and TradeFinex Tech, supports the growth of the XDC Network ecosystem across the Asia-Pacific region.
The initiative addresses a fundamental challenge in cross-border trade: how to establish trust in counterparties and transaction data while providing SMEs with faster access to working capital. By digitizing corporate verification, KYB/KYC, receivables verification, and financing processes, the solution demonstrates how digital trust infrastructure can reduce friction in international trade and financial transactions.
useCases.userJourney:
In this PoC, TOPPAN’s corporate digital certificate, the vLEI, was integrated with a digital trade application developed by SBI XDC Network APAC. Using historical transaction data from SS Trading Co., Ltd., an SBI Group company engaged in used automobile and auto parts exports, the PoC demonstrated vLEI-based corporate identity verification and the recording and verification of receivables information through the digital trade application.
The PoC confirmed that vLEI can automate online corporate identity verification for counterparties such as overseas buyers, including verification of the legal entity and its authorized representatives. It also confirmed that the authenticity and integrity of recorded receivables information can be verified through cryptographic validation of the associated vLEI.
The initiative is ongoing, with the aim of extending these capabilities to credit screening and financing and ultimately enabling the entire factoring process—from corporate identity and receivables verification through credit screening and financing—to be conducted digitally and online.

useCases.title: From Mine Permit to Digital Product Passport: Building an Open Digital Trust Ecosystem for Responsible Critical Minerals
useCases.summary:
The Mines Digital Trust initiative shows how trusted digital credentials can connect regulatory, sustainability and supply-chain evidence without forcing organizations onto a proprietary platform. Critical-mineral evidence is spread across government, mining companies, assurance programs and technology providers, making it hard for buyers, regulators and investors to verify that claims are authentic, current and linked to the material.

The solution combines a production-issued British Columbia Mines Act Permit credential, a United Nations Transparency Protocol (UNTP) digital product passport, and verifiable sustainability credentials such as Towards Sustainable Mining and The Copper Mark. Together they form an interoperable evidence chain, independently verifiable with open standards.

Digital wallets issue, hold, discover, exchange and verify credentials across platforms, including OrgBook BC and enterprise wallets. Verifiable Credentials prove origin, integrity, status and authority while each organization keeps control of its own data. The result is greater transparency, lower verification cost, better market access, privacy and a reusable digital-trust model for supply chains.

issuers.labelRaw: BC Ministry of Mines and Critical Minerals

organizations.labelRaw: Ministry of Mining and Critical Minerals

useCases.userJourney:
The Government of British Columbia issues a digital Mines Act Permit credential with authoritative permit data and publishes it through OrgBook BC, so it can be independently verified while remaining under government authority.

A mining company then creates a United Nations Transparency Protocol (UNTP) raw-material digital product passport. The passport does not copy the underlying records; it links to trusted credentials from the organizations that own them. Sustainability bodies such as Towards Sustainable Mining and The Copper Mark can add verifiable conformity credentials, forming one connected evidence chain. Each party keeps control of its own data.

Digital wallets issue, publish, exchange, discover and manage these credentials across platforms, including OrgBook BC and enterprise wallets such as Northern Block Orbit.

When a buyer, regulator, investor or supply-chain partner reviews the passport, a verifier application follows the links, confirms the issuer, checks the digital signature and integrity, and validates credential status. Government speaks for permits, mining companies for provenance, and assurance bodies for sustainability claims.

useCases.title: Autofill Customer ID on Trip.com with Google Wallet
useCases.summary: Travellers can securely share authorised identity information from an ID Pass in Google Wallet to automatically populate the passenger details required when booking a flight on Trip.com. This removes the need to enter personal and travel document information manually, making the booking process faster and more convenient. It also reduces typing errors and discrepancies between the booking and the traveller's identity document, which can otherwise cause issues during check-in or boarding. The result is a smoother booking experience, more accurate passenger data and greater user control over what information is shared. This mobility use case is submitted by Hopae and involves Trip.com as the relying party.
useCases.userJourney:
1. On Trip.com, the user selects their preferred flight and proceeds to the booking page.
2. On the Passenger Details page, the user selects Share from Wallet.
3. Android displays the digital credential selector, showing the identity credentials that can be used with Trip.com.
4. The user selects their ID Pass from Google Wallet.
5. The user reviews the information requested by Trip.com, selects Share, and authenticates using their device.
6. Google Wallet securely shares the requested information with Trip.com, and the relevant passenger details are automatically populated.
7. The user reviews the populated details and continues with the booking.

useCases.title: Business Wallet-Based KYB & Financial Onboarding
useCases.summary:
A company representative opens a business bank account in an EU member state where the company is not registered, using verified credentials from an EU Business Wallet instead of uploaded documents. 

KYB today is manual, document-based and national: banks chase register extracts across jurisdictions, verify signing authority and ownership by hand, onboarding runs to days or weeks at high cost and drop-off, and forged documents remain a fraud vector. Here the founder presents a Legal Person Identification Data credential and a European Company Certificate, plus a PID or mandate proving authority to act. Issuers are national business registers and competent authorities such as PRH in Finland; the holder is the company through an authorised representative; the verifier is the bank or fintech; Hovi provides the issuance and verification layer; supervisors and EU trust lists anchor trust. 

The wallet is the consent point, showing who is asking and for what, and releasing only approved attributes through selective disclosure. The result is same-day onboarding, register-sourced data, a stronger AML audit trail and one pattern that works across all 27 member states.
useCases.userJourney:
1. The founder starts a business account application on the bank or fintech platform and selects "verify with EU Business Wallet" instead of uploading documents.

2. The platform sends a presentation request through Hovi's verification layer, specifying the attributes required for KYB and AML.

3. The request reaches the wallet. Delivery can be triggered in-session by QR or deep link, or out of band by email or SMS, and can be combined with national eID authentication such as FTN or BankID where required.

4. The founder reviews the request in the wallet: who is asking, which attributes, for what purpose.

5. On approval, the wallet presents the LPID and ECC credentials, plus the representative's PID or mandate, over OID4VP in SD-JWT VC or mdoc format with selective disclosure.

6. The verification layer checks issuer signatures, credential validity and revocation status, and the issuer's presence on the EU trust list, then returns a structured, verified result to the platform.

7. The platform completes KYB, screens the disclosed ownership data against AML requirements, and provisions the account. The verification result is retained as an audit record.

useCases.title: Preventing SIM Swap Fraud with EUDI Wallets and AI Voice Agents
useCases.summary:
Telcos handle some of the most sensitive account actions over the phone, especially SIM swaps, which are a primary vector for account takeover fraud. This usecase shows an AI voice agent that verifies a caller's identity against a digital wallet credential in real time, before any sensitive change is processed.

SIM swap fraud, phishing, and account takeover attacks all depend on the same weak point: phone-based identity checks that rely on security questions, personal data, or callback procedures, all of which can be socially engineered or leaked. Call center agents have no reliable way to confirm that the person on the line is who they claim to be, and attackers exploit exactly that gap.

For the telco, this closes the fraud gap without adding friction for legitimate customers. Verification happens automatically, mid-conversation, with no extra steps for the caller and no manual escalation for the agent. For the customer, it means sensitive requests are protected without the hassle of extra security questions or callback delays. For the industry more broadly, it demonstrates a reusable pattern for binding any high-risk transaction to a verified identity in real time.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Customer calls in. A customer contacts the telco to request a sensitive account change, for example a SIM swap.

2. AI voice agent picks up. The agent handles the call naturally, like a normal support conversation, and asks for the details of the request.

3. Identity binding happens mid-call. Before the agent proceeds, it binds the request to the customer's verified identity credential in real time. No security questions, no callback, no manual agent escalation.

4. Dashboard tracks the call live. A real-time dashboard shows each stage of the interaction as it happens: call received, identity check triggered, verification result, outcome.

5. Verification gates the outcome. If the identity check passes, the account change goes through. If it fails, the change is blocked on the spot, before any damage is done.

6.Loyalty credential issued. Once verified, the customer receives a loyalty credential as a reward for completing a secure interaction.

This flow removes the exact weak point that SIM swap attacks, phishing, and account takeover fraud rely on: social engineering and leaked personal data used to impersonate a real customer over the phone.

useCases.title: Buy Age-Restricted Goods Online in Seconds with EUDI Wallets
useCases.summary:
Buying age-restricted products online, like alcohol, still typically means uploading a passport scan and waiting for manual review, a slow and privacy-invasive process for both the customer and the retailer. This demo shows how an EUDI Wallet turns that into a checkout step that takes seconds, without disclosing any private information like date of birth.

Online retailers selling age-restricted goods have no fast, reliable way to confirm a buyer's age at checkout. Manual document review is slow, costly to operate, and requires customers to hand over far more personal data (full passport scans) than the transaction actually needs, just to prove one fact: that they are over 18.

For the retailer, age verification becomes instant and automated, removing manual review costs and reducing checkout drop-off. For the customer, there are no forms, no document uploads, and no waiting, just a quick scan and confirmation. For the ecosystem, it shows that minimal-disclosure verification (proving only "over 18" rather than full identity) is achievable today with wallets already in production, like France Identité.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Marie shops online. She adds gin and vodka, both age-restricted products, to her cart on an online store.

2. Checkout triggers age verification. At checkout, the store requests proof that Marie is over 18 before the order can proceed.

3. Marie scans a QR code. The store displays a QR code linked to the verification request.

4. Marie completes the check in her wallet app. She scans the code with her France Identité EUDI Wallet, reviews the request, and approves sharing only her age attribute.

5. Verification completes instantly. The wallet returns a verifiable proof of age to the retailer in real time.

6. Order is confirmed. With age confirmed, the order goes through immediately, no forms, no document upload, no manual review wait.

useCases.title: Hypersign KYB — Instant Business Verification & UBO Due Diligence
useCases.summary:
BoostN is a sports fintech specializing in fundraising for the Bavarian Ice Hockey League, giving sponsors a simple way to manage their tax submissions. 

Hypermine & BoostN demonstrate a practical, privacy-preserving approach to reusable KYB verification. While basic business wallets only establish company identity, robust Know Your Business (KYB) demands multi-layered due diligence — UBO (Ultimate Beneficial Owner) verification, representative-level business KYC, PEP and sanctions screening, and full lifecycle tracking. 

Verification & Issuance : A sponsor company and its representative complete full KYC/KYB via Hypermine. On approval, Hypermine issues a non-qualified W3C Verifiable Credential directly to the sponsor's Company Vault. 

Independent Relying-Party Validation : BoostN, as the relying party, requests onboarding evidence. The sponsor presents the credential, letting BoostN independently verify cryptographic integrity, issuer trust, freshness, credential revocation status, and policy rules — before granting access. 

Impact : Eliminates repetitive onboarding and document sharing, preserving enterprise control, relying-party sovereignty, and verifiable auditability.
useCases.userJourney:
KYB Verification & Reusable Credential Flow

01 — Opportunity & Request: Sponsor A selects an opportunity on BoostN, triggering company KYB and representative KYC verifications.

02 — Due Diligence: The representative submits company, UBO, and identity data via Hypermine, which executes ownership analysis, sanctions/PEP screening, and risk-based onboarding checks against verification policies.

03 — Credential Issuance: Upon approval, Hypermine issues a reusable W3C Verifiable Credential (KYB Credential) to Sponsor A’s Company Vault, embedding identifiers, performed checks, policy details, validity periods, and revocation mechanisms.

04 — Consent & Presentation: BoostN issues a purpose-bound data request. Sponsor A reviews and explicitly authorizes credential presentation directly from its vault via built-in consent management.

05 — Verification & Decision: BoostN cryptographically validates Hypermine’s signature, integrity, policy compliance, freshness, and revocation status before finalizing the onboarding decision.

06 — Reusability: Sponsor A retains the reusable KYB credential in its vault for instant reuse across other relying parties — no repeat due diligence.

useCases.title: Flow! - A seamless digital journey for bereaved people
useCases.summary:
After a death, bereaved people face an overwhelming number of administrative obligations at a time when grief can reduce their cognitive capacity. Fragmented processes make this harder: information and proof must be repeatedly provided to government agencies, banks and insurers. Physical documents create an additional burden and can delay the settlement of an estate.
Flow! explores how eIDAS 2.0 and the European Digital Identity Wallet can make this journey simpler, more user- and privacy-friendly. The project focuses on making two essential documents available in the wallet: the Death Certificate and the Certificate of Inheritance. This allows bereaved people to share only the data specifically required, instead of submitting complete documents. It reduces administrative burden while giving people greater control over their data.
Flow! redesigns the entire journey, rather than simply adding a wallet to existing processes. The Death Certificate solution is ready for implementation, with a blueprint that municipalities can use to unlock other documents in the same way. The Certificate of Inheritance requires legislative and notarial process changes and is being further developed.

organizations.labelRaw: Ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties

useCases.userJourney:
The demo follows Froukje Jansen, a fictional bereaved person whose father, Jan Klaassen, has died. In the redesigned MijnOverheid, Froukje has one central place to manage both public and private matters related to the death.
After logging in with her ID Wallet, she receives a clear step-by-step overview of what needs to be arranged. A condolence message and reassurance that no mandatory government actions are required during the first three months provide immediate peace of mind. Notifications and support can be switched on or off, giving Froukje control over the process.
The ID Wallet enables her to retrieve the Death Certificate and Certificate of Inheritance directly from the issuing authorities and store them digitally. She can then share only the minimum data required with organisations such as insurers and banks, eliminating paper documents, PDFs and lengthy forms.
The demo also shows how verified data can provide rapid access to vehicle registrations and enable funeral costs to be paid without unnecessary delay. Froukje can pause at any time and continue later, with her progress saved in MijnOverheid. This allows her to manage the process at her own pace, when she is ready.

useCases.title: Digital Twin based Verifiable Credentials for local impact, proven on the Open Interop Testbed
useCases.summary:
itb.ilabs.ai is in production: a GITB test bed operated by iLabs, with external accounts, listed on fides.community as the Open Interop Testbed. It is where LDT4SSC/EUTwinLink wallets, issuers and verifiers prove they interoperate.

What runs on it matters locally. Local impact is rewarded on trust, or not at all: carbon methodologies are built around reduction, avoidance or removal of greenhouse gases, so they exclude coral restoration, beach cleaning, water conservation, and the resilience work that counts most in a small island economy, such as making the homes of elderly residents safer, warmer and cheaper to run.

LDT4SSC makes that impact spendable where it is earned, over three layers. The Local Digital Twin holds the ground truth: place, time, sensor, audit trail. The data space (iSHARE) moves it between city, project owner and retailer under agreed rules. The verifiable credential makes anyone believe it.

The testbed holds the three together. Every party runs the DIIP v5 suite and receives a signed report with a resolvable link; issuing that report as a Conformance Test Report credential is next in development. Interoperability here is a suite that can be watched fail.
useCases.userJourney:
1. A wallet, issuer or verifier joining the ecosystem opens an account on itb.ilabs.ai and runs the DIIP v5 suite against its endpoints.

2. The test bed runs the suite and produces a signed GITB test report with link: session id, suite version, date, verdict per test case.

3. Next in development: issuing that report as a Conformance Test Report credential over OpenID4VCI, carrying the PASS verdict, suite version, session id and a resolvable link to the signed report, so anyone can open the evidence in one click.

4. A resident or project owner completes a verified local action: a CO2 reduction, a coral restoration, a household energy improvement.

5. The Local Digital Twin records it against a place, time and sensor, with the evidence and audit trail.

6. The LDT4SSC issuer (co2-token-issuer.ldt4ssc.tech) issues a CO2 measurement token over OpenID4VCI, per DIIP v5, to the holder's wallet.

7. The holder presents it over OpenID4VP to the EU LDT Marketplace, a municipal scheme or a retailer, which checks signature, status and validity before recognising it, and may require the counterparty's Test Report credential first.

useCases.title: Instant Digital Verification of Education Credentials using VerifyTT
useCases.summary: VerifyTT is Trinidad and Tobago's national platform for issuing, holding, and verifying digital credentials, starting with academic certificates and extending to legal and official documents. It solves the problem of paper credentials being fragile, slow to trust, and hard to verify, since confirming authenticity often means contacting the issuer. This costs graduates time, leaves employers uncertain, and burdens institutions with repeat verification requests. VerifyTT creates value for all: holders get a record safe from loss, fire, or flood; employers get instant "Blue Tick" verification; issuers spend less time on manual work. Institutions act as issuers, digitally signing credentials at source. Citizens are holders, claiming credentials via email and controlling who sees them. Employers act as verifiers, checking authenticity in seconds. The digital wallet lets holders securely store and selectively share credentials from their phone, shifting control to the individual. Verifiable credentials, cryptographically signed by the issuer, make instant trust possible: a QR scan checks a tamper-proof signature, not a document's look, enabling verification without contacting the issuer.

useCases.title: Tax Splitter: real-time VAT collection with verifiable organisational identity
useCases.summary:
The European Commission estimates the annual EU VAT gap at EUR 128 billion (2023). At the same time, Dutch entrepreneurs spend 30 to 40 hours per year on VAT administration. Both problems share a root cause: tax compliance happens after the fact, through declarations, reconciliation and audits.

Tax Splitter turns that around. Every transaction automatically splits the VAT amount and transfers it directly to the tax authority at the moment of payment. A business owner no longer needs to reserve, calculate or declare VAT. The invoice is the return.

The mechanism is digital trust. Organisations hold verifiable credentials (issued by Credenco) in organisational wallets, so every payment starts with an identity lookup: is the counterparty a real, registered business or a shell company? The payment itself carries a cryptographic reference to the invoice, creating an audit trail that all parties can verify without exposing the underlying data: proofs are shared, not the records themselves. Each party keeps control of its own data; the infrastructure moves sealed envelopes, it never looks inside. Parties that don't share databases share cryptographic proof instead.

The system was developed over two years by the Dutch Tax Authority (Directorate Control and Finance, problem owner), mintBlue (infrastructure and development) and Credenco (verifiable credentials and digital identity), through a Design Sprint and two completed development phases. It runs as a proof of concept with a working end-to-end demonstration: visitors buy a product at a point-of-sale system, pay with a wallet, and watch the VAT split and settle in real-time. A pilot with real entrepreneurs is in preparation, and the tax authority has driven the project itself at every step, from the design sprint to the working demonstration.

In March 2026, Tax Splitter won the Innovation Award of the Dutch Ministry of Finance. The OECD cites the project in its Tax Administration Series as an inspiring example of real-time tax collection. Where the EU's ViDA legislation (VAT in the Digital Age) introduces real-time reporting from 2028, Tax Splitter goes one step further and collects the tax as the payment happens.

The same pattern applies to any predictable levy. The partners are exploring gambling tax, property transfer tax, excise duties, tourist levies and cross-border VAT, where the tax automatically reaches the tax authority of the right country. The approach is drawing interest from tax authorities in the United Kingdom and Scandinavia.
useCases.userJourney:
1. In the proof of concept, a seller issues an invoice. Before any money moves, the buyer's system performs an identity lookup on the seller's verifiable organisational credential, issued by Credenco. The check rejects shell companies before the payment can start.

2. The buyer pays from an organisational wallet, at a point-of-sale terminal or online. The wallet holds the organisation's credentials, so every payment is bound to a verified legal identity.

3. At the moment of payment the amount splits automatically: the net amount settles with the seller, the VAT portion transfers directly to the tax authority's wallet. No one has to set money aside or file anything.

4. The payment carries a cryptographic reference to the underlying invoice. Invoice and payment are verifiably linked in a single audit trail that all parties can check without exposing the underlying business data to anyone else.

5. The tax authority follows VAT flows in real-time through its portal and handles settlement and refunds over the same infrastructure. Discrepancies surface immediately instead of months after a quarterly declaration.

6. The entrepreneur does nothing: no reserving, no calculating, no declaring. The invoice is the return.

The demonstration is a simplified consumer version of this business-to-business flow: at a physical point-of-sale setup, visitors buy a product, pay with a demonstration wallet, and see the VAT reach the tax authority's wallet on the spot.

useCases.title: Recomputable carbon intensity for gold doré bars
useCases.summary:
Gold leaves the mine as doré bars, and every buyer — refiner, trader, and soon every EU importer under CBAM — asks how much CO2 the bar embodies. Today the answer is a consultant's PDF: it can't be independently checked or partially disclosed.

For each doré bar we issue two SD-JWT verifiable credentials a third party can check without trusting the issuer: an origin credential (identity, mass, fineness, lot), self-issued by the mine (AGM, Aurora, Guyana) from a did:web on its own domain; and a carbon-intensity credential issued by Natixar (kgCO2e per kg fine gold), bound to it.

The holder discloses selectively — proving purity, mass or the carbon figure without revealing the site or commercial data. A public page resolves the issuer's key from its own domain, verifies the signature, the disclosed-data integrity and revocation status — no account, no call back to us. Tampered, revoked and replayed presentations are rejected.

Value: a carbon figure that survives contradiction — the buyer checks it without trusting the calculator; the mine shows what a contract requires and no more.

useCases.title: Neoflow Digital Energy Passport for Cross-Border Crude Oil Clearance

Neoflow operates a digital rail for energy traceability across the Canada-U.S. border. Every batch of crude oil crossing by pipeline now carries a verifiable Digital Passport built with a set of W3C verifiable credentials proving, in real time, who owns it, where it came from, what it is, and where it sits.  

Today, a single batch of crude oil passes through 100-plus documents and 15-plus parties before clearing customs and it takes 45-90 days to do so, after the barrels have crossed the border. Furthermore, Importers who cannot prove USMCA origin may face tariffs.  

Neoflow solves this by issuing and consolidating W3C verifiable credentials at the batch level across its lifecycle, built on open VCDM and DID standards. Companies issue their own data, Neoflow holds and presents it, CBP verifies. Every credential is cryptographically signed, so origin clears digitally and cuts tariff exposure. 

Neoflow is live since July 2nd, 2026 and accounting for close to 25% of all oil flows from Canada into the US allowing crude oil importers to seamlessly share information about their products with US Customs and Border Protection.

useCases.title: Age Verification by SnapKYC
useCases.summary:
SnapKYC is a consent-based verification orchestrator that lets a relying party confirm a user meets an eligibility requirement, such as an age threshold, without storing or exposing personal data.
It holds no credentials of its own. Built on open identity standards, it requests an eligibility claim from an existing trusted source. Today that source is Aadhaar, via the Aadhaar app and DigiLocker, and the same approach lets other issuers or wallets be added without changing the relying party's integration.
When content is tagged age-restricted, the viewer is asked to verify their age. With their consent, SnapKYC sends an age-eligibility request to Aadhaar and receives only a yes or no. No age, date of birth, or identity attribute reaches the platform, and SnapKYC retains nothing. Age thresholds are configurable by jurisdiction, so one flow covers different regional age-of-majority rules.
Shown here through a media interface built to demonstrate the flow, not a live integration. Key players: UIDAI as issuer, the Aadhaar app as credential wallet, and SnapKYC as the verification layer any platform could adopt as a relying party. It is currently a working prototype.
useCases.userJourney:
1: Access Age-Restricted Content: A user attempts to access content designated as age-restricted on a social media platform.
2: Age Verification Prompt: Before proceeding, the user is prompted to verify their age. On a web browser, this can be initiated by scanning a QR code; within a mobile app, the user can initiate the credential-sharing flow directly.
3: Privacy-Preserving Age Check: SnapKYC requests an age-eligibility claim from the user’s Aadhaar-linked wallet in real time. The eligibility check is based on the applicable age threshold for the user’s jurisdiction—for example, 16+ or 18+.
4: Minimal Data Disclosure: The verification returns only a Yes/No eligibility response. SnapKYC does not share the user’s date of birth, name, Aadhaar number, or other identity information with the social media platform.
5: Seamless Continuation: If the user meets the required age threshold, they are returned to the exact content they were attempting to access.
6: Access Restricted: If the user does not meet the required threshold, they are informed that the content is unavailable based on the applicable age requirement and are redirected to the platform’s home screen.

useCases.title: Verifiable Work-Completion Credentials for Migrant Construction Workers
useCases.summary:
India's Building and Other Construction Workers (BOCW) scheme entitles a migrant construction worker to welfare benefits once they complete 90 days of work in a year. The hard part was proving it. Eligibility rested on paper: forms, signatures, and manual checks that were slow for workers and hard for officials to verify. Paper is also easy to forge, and fabricated work histories are a known weak point in welfare disbursal, so those who genuinely qualify are often the hardest to believe.
Jan Sahas set out to close that gap. With construction firms Ashiana Housing and Total Environment, it piloted a verifiable alternative built on CredIssuer, Ooru's verifiable credentials ecosystem. Site administrators log each worker's history into a Worker Registry; entries are approved in real time, and once a worker has enough approved days, a tamper-resistant digital certificate with a QR code is issued. The worker attaches it to their BOCW application, and a labour official confirms it in seconds through CredIssuer's portal instead of checking paperwork by hand.
The flow is live. In the pilot, 194 certificates were issued and verified, enabling workers to gain faster access to their benefits.
useCases.userJourney:
1: A site administrator logs each worker's work history into the Worker Registry.
2: The registered contractor of the site the worker worked on reviews and approves each entry in real time.
3: Once a worker reaches 90 approved days, CredIssuer issues a verified certificate with an embedded QR code.
4: The worker adds it to their BOCW application, and a labour official verifies it by scanning the QR code through CredIssuer's portal.

useCases.title: IIIT-Bangalore Digital Academic Credential Issuance and Verification
useCases.summary:
A degree is only as useful as the world's ability to trust it. For a graduate, proving one has long meant waiting while an employer or verification agency writes to the university and staff check the paperwork by hand, a slow step that can hold up a job.
IIIT-Bangalore now issues degree certificates and transcripts as verifiable credentials through CredIssuer (by Ooru), organised by batch and programme across online and offline cohorts. Background verification (BGV) agencies confirm them through a custom verification portal built by CredIssuer. If a credential carries a QR code, the check completes automatically once the fee is paid. If it does not, the system runs an OCR match against IIIT-B's verifiable records, and an IIIT-B reviewer manually approves or rejects it with a recorded comment. Automation carries the routine cases; a person handles the rest.
The system is live in production. Issuance began in 2025 and verification in 2026, with 10,485 credentials issued and 197 verifications to date. IIIT-B is issuer and verifier; BGV agencies are the relying parties. No personal wallet is active yet, though CredIssuer's architecture supports one.
useCases.userJourney:
1. IIIT-Bangalore issues degree certificates and transcripts as verifiable credentials through CredIssuer, organised by batch and programme.
2. A BGV agency needing to confirm a candidate's credentials logs into the custom verification portal built by CredIssuer.
3. The agency submits the candidate's credentials, with or without an embedded QR code (legacy credentials), and pays the verification fee.
4. If a QR code is present, verification completes automatically once payment is made.
5. If no QR code is present, the system runs an OCR match to find the corresponding verifiable credentials, and the IIIT-B team manually reviews and approves or rejects the request, with a mandatory comment.
6. The BGV agency receives the verified result, completing the hiring-related check.

useCases.title: Digitising Police Clearance Certificates with DGRN, São Tomé & Príncipe
useCases.summary:
A Police Clearance Certificate is something a citizen of São Tomé & Príncipe cannot do without. It is asked for at almost every threshold that matters: a job, a university place, a visa, a scholarship, studying or working abroad. It is still collected in person, on paper, at a DGRN counter. The hard part was never obtaining it. It was proving it was genuine, since anyone receiving it had to take it on trust.
DGRN, set out to close that gap. The certificate is still issued at the counter, but it is now issued as a verifiable credential with a QR code, so anyone who receives it can confirm it is genuine in seconds, anywhere in the world. 
DGRN issues and stands behind each certificate, checking the applicant against the joint government criminal record database first. CredIssuer, Ooru's credentials ecosystem, turns a cleared record into a tamper-evident verifiable certificate. Verifica (https://verifica.gov.st/), Ooru's public verification portal for the country, is where universities, employers, and government bodies confirm it is real. This flow is live today. The next phase adds a citizen-facing portal and wallet, and lets DGRN design and deploy these credential forms itself.
useCases.userJourney:
1: A citizen applies for a Police Clearance Certificate at DGRN and states the reason for the request, such as employment, a visa, or education. That reason is recorded directly in the certificate.
2: DGRN checks the applicant against the joint government criminal record database.
3: Where the record is clear, DGRN calls CredIssuer to generate the certificate as a verifiable credential with an embedded QR code.
4: The certificate is issued to the citizen on the spot, with no change to the existing application process. This part of the flow is live today.
5: The citizen presents the certificate to whoever requires it: a university, an employer, or a government body, at home or abroad.
6: The relying party confirms it is genuine through the Verifica portal (https://verifica.gov.st/), by scanning the QR code, uploading the document, or looking up the credential ID.

useCases.title: PASS2RENT: From Proof of Age to Open Door — Car Rental on EUDI Wallets
useCases.summary:
PASS2RENT demonstrates how EUDI Wallets can support an entire car-rental journey with privacy-preserving, interoperable credentials.

At booking, the driver proves the required age through the wallet. The rental platform receives only the driver's name and an age_over_18 result, not the birth date. At the vehicle, a mobile driving licence identifies the driver through a fresh, holder-bound presentation. No counter visit, photocopy or ID scan is required.

One in-house OpenID4VP verifier handles every interaction and accepted both France Identité and the European Commission's EUDI reference wallet without wallet-specific integration. Any birth date used to derive an age result is discarded within milliseconds and never reaches a database, API or webhook. The design also includes a tamper-evident audit trail with no personal data, encryption at rest, strict retention and erasure controls.

Demonstrated end to end, the use case shows that EUDI Wallets can replace document collection with selective disclosure and reusable, standards-based verification across different wallets and credential types.
useCases.userJourney:
https://api.playground.france-identite.gouv.fr/odifis/contactless-rent/en/

1. Booking. The driver selects a car and scans a QR code with France Identité. The rental platform receives only age_over_18: true. Any birth date disclosed to the verifier is discarded within milliseconds and never reaches the platform, its database or an API.

2. Identification. At the car, the driver presents a test mobile driving licence from the EU reference wallet, or uses the PID as a fallback. The same verifier checks the credential and shares only the structured claims needed for the rental—no scans or document images.

3. Handover. A fresh, device-bound presentation answers a dynamic challenge. After verification, the platform issues a short-lived, replay-protected token. Only a pseudonymous handover record and the verification method are retained.

4. Data minimisation. The database stores the age result, required rental claims and a pseudonymous attestation. It does not store a birth date, portrait, licence image or photocopy.

5. Trust. Credentials are checked against recognised trust anchors and revocation sources. Unknown issuers are flagged, never silently accepted.

useCases.title: HIMS eSPA - Electronic Sale and Purchase Agreement using Digital Signature
useCases.summary:

Pos Digicert is the issuer, iDsaya the holder and HIMS the verifier. The credential contains a pseudonymous ID, role, transaction reference, issuance and expiry dates.
Achieved outcomes: eSPA enables secure remote verification and legally recognised signing, reducing processing time, paperwork and physical visits while protecting document integrity. JWT VC strengthens participant and role verification without replacing PKI-based signing.

useCases.title: Portable Volunteer Credentials
useCases.summary:
In Japan, proof of volunteer activity is scattered across paper rosters, spreadsheets, and organization-specific ledgers. Volunteers rarely keep durable evidence, and schools and employers who value civic engagement cannot confirm a submitted record is genuine.
This use case solves that with verifiable credentials. JAVO (NPO JAPAN Volunteer Association), a nonprofit normalizing volunteering in Japan, acts as a neutral third-party issuer that independently reviews and approves each certificate, giving it credibility beyond any single organization. Recept provides the infrastructure through its DID/VC platform proovy (OEM), whose SaaS powers both issuance and verification.
Volunteers receive their certificate into the proovy wallet and own it for life. They present it with selective disclosure to universities, employers, or other programs, and any verifier instantly confirms the content and JAVO's endorsement. Applications span community service, environmental work, disaster preparedness, and education.
The impact: individuals gain lasting, portable recognition for their contribution, institutions can trust and reward it, and low-friction proof helps grow volunteering in Japan.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Activity record. A volunteer takes part in an activity (community service, environmental work, disaster preparedness, education, etc.); the host organization submits the participation record to JAVO.
2. Independent review. JAVO, as a neutral third party, reviews and approves the content of the certificate — establishing trust beyond any single organization.
3. Issuance. JAVO issues a verifiable volunteer certificate to the volunteer through the proovy platform (OpenID4VCI).
4. Hold in the wallet. The volunteer stores the credential in the proovy wallet on their smartphone and owns it permanently, independent of any single organization's records.
5. Present with selective disclosure. When applying to a university, a job, or another program, the volunteer presents the credential (OpenID4VP), sharing only the attributes needed.
6. Instant verification. The relying party cryptographically verifies the credential and confirms JAVO's third-party endorsement — no phone calls, no paper, no doubt about authenticity.

useCases.title: Reeco Textile DPP : the supply chain verified independently of the brand's systems
useCases.summary:
Textile passports today publish what a brand exports from its PLM. A signature makes that tamper-evident, not true. Reeco verifies the chain itself, from outside the brand's systems: every supplier lodges its documents directly with Reeco, and a proprietary mass balance, carrying the indices and the PEF calculation, bounds each claim to its certified evidence. No signed claim survives in excess of what the certificates cover.
The passport is issued from that result: a W3C Verifiable Credential from did:web:ia.reeco.eco, delivered over OpenID4VCI to an organisational or personal wallet, presented back over OpenID4VP and verified against the published DID document, eleven checks including holder key binding. Verification is the product; the passport is what verification leaves behind.
There is a date on this. From 27 September 2026, Directive (EU) 2024/825 makes a generic environmental claim an unfair practice: only specific, substantiated claims survive, and substantiation is not a publishing problem.
No textile DPP can be conforming yet: the delegated act is not adopted and service providers cannot register. This is a pilot, and says so. The stack is live and public.
useCases.userJourney:
1. A brand declares the composition and sustainability claims for a production lot and
   supplies the supply-chain documents for each tier.
2. Before anything is signed, Reeco checks the declared claim against the certified
   evidence. If the evidence does not support the claim, the passport is not issued at the
   declared value.
3. The passport is issued as a UNTP 0.7.0 Verifiable Credential signed with Ed25519, with
   a GS1 Digital Link identifier at unit level (AI 01 / 10 / 21) as its subject id.
4. A consumer scans the QR on the garment. The GS1 Digital Link resolver returns the
   passport in a plain-language view; the credential status is resolved live, so a
   superseded or revoked claim never reads as valid.
5. A repairer or recycler reads material and end-of-life data from the same identifier.
6. A market surveillance authority retrieves the same passport, verifies the signature
   against the published DID document, and can retrieve the archived version from the
   independent back-up service if the primary is unavailable.

useCases.title: Verifiable Participant Identity for Cross-Border Financial Messaging
useCases.summary:
RTGS.global is a live SaaS platform coordinating cross-border FX and payment workflows between participating financial institutions, including banks, fund controllers, financial market infrastructures and central banks across jurisdictions.

RTGS.global provides the shared operating and messaging layer through which participants establish governed relationships and coordinate payment workflows. It operates without holding participant funds or acting as an authoritative settlement record; institutions maintain their own records and external settlement arrangements.

The trust challenge is ensuring that every institution communicating across the network is reliably identified and that all instructions are authenticated and tamper-evident. Traditional static certificates cannot satisfy this dynamically across distributed participants. RTGS.global solves this by embedding verifiable institutional identity into every communication and financial message across its network.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Onboarding: RTGS.global emails a single-use out-of-band invitation. The participant's managed Aries agent loads it at container startup to establish a peer-to-peer connection via DIDComm v1. DIDs and credential definitions are anchored on Hyperledger Indy.
2. Credential issuance: RTGS.global issues an AnonCreds credential binding institutional attributes to the participant's managed agent wallet.
3. Proof verification: The participant presents a zero-knowledge proof of credential possession. RTGS.global verifies the proof and checks revocation status before activating the connection.
4. Message signing: Active connections use pairwise DIDs. Every enabled financial message is cryptographically signed by the sending agent using relationship-specific keys.
5. Verification: The receiving service validates the signature against the connection key, confirming the authenticated sender and intended recipient before processing.
6. Lifecycle: Trust maintenance is automated via scheduled and DIDComm-instructed key cycling, connection cleanup, credential updates and offboarding.
