useCases.title: Reusable KYC on open standards: verify once, present anywhere, re-collect nothing
useCases.summary:
A person completes identity verification once, receives a verifiable credential they hold themselves, and presents it to any number of independent verifiers without re-submitting documents. Each verifier learns only the attributes it actually needs.

Solidus Network implements this on multi-stakeholder open standards rather than a proprietary format: W3C Verifiable Credentials 2.0, SD-JWT VC with holder key binding, OpenID4VCI for issuance, OpenID4VP with Presentation Exchange for presentation, BBS+ for selective disclosure, StatusList for revocation, and DIDComm v2 routing through a full mediator. The did:solidus method is registered in the W3C DID Method Registry, which is a registry listing rather than a W3C standard or endorsement.

The implementation is open source and published on npm under @solidus-network, so a credential issued here is readable by any conformant wallet or verifier, and the tooling is reusable by anyone building the same thing rather than rebuilding it.

It runs today on a public testnet. The wallet is in beta. There is no production deployment and no external security audit.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Issue. The holder verifies their identity at verify.solidus.network, which reads a passport or national ID document (ICAO 9303 MRZ and NFC chip). On success the issuer mints a KYCVerified credential over OpenID4VCI, in W3C VC 2.0 and SD-JWT VC formats, cryptographically bound to the holder's key.

2. Hold. The credential is delivered to the holder's wallet at wallet.solidus.network, in beta on testnet. The holder's identity keys are did:solidus DIDs. Revocation status is published as a StatusList.

3. Present. A second relying party requests a presentation over OpenID4VP, stating its requirements as a Presentation Exchange presentation_definition. The wallet answers with a BBS+ selective-disclosure proof that reveals only the requested attributes, withholds the rest of the credential, and proves holder binding.

4. Result. The second party is satisfied without collecting the document and without contacting the first. No second copy of the passport is created.

The issuer metadata is public at verify.solidus.network/.well-known/openid-credential-issuer.

useCases.title: Verified machine safety access at Koning Willem I College (KW1C)
useCases.summary:
A student is trained on a high-risk workshop machine and receives a digital machine safety certificate. That same digital certificate lets the student book the machine online. Later, at the machine itself, the student holds their credential against the machine's reader. The same certificate is checked again, and only then does the physical lock release.

Most digital identity projects stay online: a credential is shown, a screen confirms it, done. This case bridges the online world and the physical world with the same credential and the same EUDI and ISO standards. Only the physical check of the certificate at the machine decides whether it runs at all. The machine either starts, or it stays locked.
useCases.userJourney:
A student completes safety training for a high-risk machine. KW1C, using its Sphereon VDX business wallet, issues a machine safety certificate as an ISO 18013-5 mdoc to the student's personal wallet.

To reserve a machine, the student logs in with their SURF eduID, which confirms they are enrolled at KW1C, and presents the safety certificate online. VDX verifies it, and only a valid certificate allows the student to make a reservation via the business wallet.

At the reserved time, the student stands at the machine and holds the same credential against the reader. VDX verifies it again, now in person over NFC/BLE. No person checks it; the machine does. 
On a successful check the existing Simac Pronto controller releases the physical lock. An unsuccessful check leaves the machine locked.

The innovation is the combination of digital and physical in one credential. The same certificate, issued once, is verified both ways: online when booking, and in person at the machine. Most digital identity stops at the screen. Here the digital reaches into the physical: it unlocks a real machine, or keeps it locked.

useCases.title: Spherity's Trusted AI
useCases.summary: Spherity Trusted AI enables autonomous AI agents to act securely within ecosystems such as Catena-X through cryptographically verifiable identities and machine-readable authorizations. It links each agent to a registered legal entity through an AI Service Passport, a narrowly scoped Power of Attorney, and a verified Corporate Identity. This creates a clear, auditable chain of accountability, allowing organisations such as Catena-X participants as well as others to verify who operates an agent, what it is permitted to do, and who is legally responsible. Aligned with eIDAS 2.0 and the EU AI Act, the service supports trusted agent interactions across industrial data spaces, regulated industries, and cross-company value chains.
useCases.userJourney:
The end-user flow establishes a verifiable trust chain for Agent-to-Agent (A2A) interactions in Catena-X ecosystems, as explored by the Catena-X Trusted AI Expert Group:

Issuance: Trusted sources, such as official business registers or Bundesanzeiger Verlag, issue corporate identity credentials, including Legal Person Identifiers, licenses, or market roles, to a company’s European Business Wallet under the eIDAS 2.0 trust framework. Additional ecosystem credentials may be issued by trusted participants or authorities.

Delegation: A company in Catena-X issues a Power of Attorney credential to an AI Agent Wallet, defining permitted actions, limitations, and validity. An AI Service Passport provides verifiable lifecycle, provenance, and compliance information.

A2A Exchange: When interacting with another Catena-X participant, the AI service agent presents its corporate identity, Power of Attorney, and AI Service Passport credentials via the Catena-X DPS/DCP Protocol.

Verification: The receiving agent verifies signatures, trusted issuers, delegated mandate, validity, and revocation status in real time. Once verified, the interaction can proceed securely and automatically.

useCases.title: Honduras: Billetera Electronica Nacional (BIEN) - 4 gob authorities issuing into one citizen-controlled wallet
useCases.summary:
Honduras launched BIEN, a self-sovereign digital identity wallet letting citizens hold and present official state credentials from their phone. Four authorities issue into one wallet: RNP (biometric national ID, DNIB) and INM (residence card for foreign residents) are the foundational trust anchors; DNVT (driving licence) and DPI/National Police (firearms permit) build on that root of trust.

Before BIEN, each document came from a different authority and could only be verified in person. The real challenge was legal standing and institutional acceptance, not digitization. Resolution No. 37,196 gave the DNIB legal equivalence to the physical ID, and institutions were instructed to accept wallet credentials within a week of launch. In month one, roughly 200,000 credentials were issued across RNP, INM, DNVT and DPI, reaching Hondurans at home and in the US.

Built on open standards (W3C Verifiable Credentials/DIDs, DIDComm v2, OIDC4VCI/VP, SD-JWT, ISO specs), BIEN stores credentials encrypted on-device, unlocked by face and password, and discloses only the fields a verifier needs. Any authority can verify offline via an encrypted 2D barcode, no internet required.

useCases.userJourney:
1. The citizen downloads BIEN free (Google Play/App Store) and registers a phone number and password.

2. They select their identity provider: RNP for Honduran nationals, INM for legal foreign residents.

3. They capture their face with the front camera. A liveness check runs first, then it's matched 1:1 against the issuing authority's own biometric record — the authority verifies the citizen, not the platform.

4. The credential is issued into the wallet in seconds as a W3C Verifiable Credential paired with a 2D barcode carrying the signature and a biometric reference, enabling fully offline verification.

5. Using that credential as proof of identity, DNVT (driving licence) and DPI/National Police (firearms permit) issue further credentials into the same wallet — no re-enrolment needed.

6. To present a credential, the citizen unlocks the wallet with face and password, then shares it offline (2D barcode, no network needed), remotely (online transactions), or by proximity (NFC/BLE).

7. The citizen sees which fields are requested and consents before sharing (selective disclosure); only needed data leaves the device. Digital and physical documents carry equal legal weight.

useCases.title: Transpareo - product truth anyone can verify
useCases.summary:
Every product makes claims - recycled, sustainable, ethically sourced, repairable - and today a shopper has no way to check any of them. Under the EU's new Digital Product Passport rules, every product will soon carry a digital record reachable from a QR code. But a record you cannot verify is just marketing with extra steps.

Transpareo makes that record a verifiable credential. Each product passport is sealed with a W3C Data Integrity proof over Ed25519 and bound to the maker's own domain through a did:web identifier. There is no wallet app to install - the passport carries itself. Scan the QR code and our open-source viewer, the Transpareo Time Machine, verifies the signature right in the browser, offline, against nothing but a public key. You are not trusting the brand, and you are not trusting us. You are checking the maths.

The impact is social: shoppers can tell real sustainability claims from marketing, repairers and recyclers get data they can trust, and regulators verify independently. Every version is kept in a foundation-owned write-once archive, so the record outlives its issuer. Live demo: https://time-machine.transpareo.com/
useCases.userJourney:
1. A maker (manufacturer or importer) creates a product passport in Transpareo and publishes it. Transpareo seals that version as a verifiable credential: a W3C Data Integrity proof over Ed25519, signed with a key bound to the maker's own domain via a did:web identifier. A GS1 Digital Link QR code on the product points to the passport.

2. A shopper scans the QR code with their phone. Nothing is installed, no wallet, no account: the link opens our open-source viewer, the Transpareo Time Machine, in the browser.

3. The viewer fetches the passport and its proof, resolves the maker's public key from the did:web identifier, and verifies the signature client-side, offline, against that key. A pass means the record is authentic and unaltered, and the shopper can verify every earlier version too.

4. A repairer or recycler later scans the same code to read repair and material data, and verifies it the same way.

5. A market-surveillance authority verifies the same passport independently through a dedicated Authority API, which logs an audit entry on every access. Each party checks from its own side, trusting the maths rather than the maker or Transpareo.

useCases.title: USA Secure Domestic Travel: TSA Mobile Driver's License at Airport Checkpoints
useCases.summary:
TSA enables domestic travelers to present a mobile driver's license (mDL) instead of a physical ID for identity verification at airport security checkpoints. Travelers get a contactless experience that shares only 6 data fields; TSA gets stronger assurance that the document is real and faster processing; issuing states lay the groundwork for a broader Digital ID ecosystem.

The use case is live. In May 2026, mDLs were presented at 271 airports, with 45,800 transactions that month. Monthly volume grew from 22,000 in March 2025 to 46,000 in May 2026. Twenty-one states and territories issue accepted credentials, presented through 13 wallet applications: Apple Wallet, Google Wallet, Samsung Wallet, and 10 state-issued apps. Each app has passed DHS/TSA requirements so the Digital ID retains REAL ID standards.

Having a lead, example Use Case for mDL acceptance has been essential to the adoption of Mobile Driver’s License in the United States.  TSA has set the example for participation by Relying Parties that accept mDL and created a level of momentum of the ecosystem that has been difficult to obtain with solely commercial Relying Parties.  Acceptance at TSA has become core requirements
useCases.userJourney:
A participating state DMV or motor vehicle agency issues an mDL that stays in the same trust chain as the physical driver's license and can carry a REAL ID indicator. The credential is provisioned into a supported wallet: Apple Wallet, Google Wallet, Samsung Wallet, or a state-issued app such as Alaska Mobile ID, California DMV Wallet, LA Wallet, NY MiD, or VA MiD.

At a TSA checkpoint, the traveler presents the mDL from their smartphone instead of a physical license. TSA, as relying party, requests only the identity attributes needed for passenger screening and receives traveler consent before any data is shared. A TSA-approved reader authenticates the credential electronically. TSA Officers use the verified identity for screening, while automated authentication and biometric matching reduce manual visual inspection.

This proximity, contactless flow is in operation at 271 airports. Verification time is 6.83 seconds versus about 20 seconds for physical ID. The same standards-based mDL can later extend to other scenarios such as age verification and government services.

useCases.title: ARIA: the trust handshake that lets any organisation verify an AI agent at its door
useCases.summary:
AI agents already buy, negotiate and file on behalf of organisations — and they cross the boundary of the company that built them. At the receiving end, almost nothing answers three questions in the moment an agent knocks: who is this, which legal entity is accountable for it, and is it still permitted to act?

ARIA answers with a trust handshake. The agent declares its credential and its intent. The receiver evaluates both against a policy it published itself, in its own DNS, then admits or refuses with a defined response code — an auditable decision, never a silent drop. Verification runs locally at the receiver.

The credential is an AID: a W3C Verifiable Credential naming the agent and the party accountable for it, signed with a post-quantum composite suite (ML-DSA-65 + Ed25519, both must verify). Revocation reaches verifiers in about sixty seconds via an append-only ledger.

The standard is stewarded by a nonprofit, not a company. Spec CC-BY-4.0, code Apache 2.0, base level free permanently. Live since April 2026: 15 active AIDs across 5 organisations, published at api.aria.bar/v1/stats. Early numbers — infrastructure described at the moment before adoption, not after it.
useCases.userJourney:
1. An operator registers its agent with the ARIA Registry and names its Principal — the legal entity accountable for what that agent does.

2. The registry issues an AID: a W3C Verifiable Credential naming the agent, its Principal and its trust level, signed with a post-quantum composite suite. It is held by the operator's systems — the holder here is a machine, not a person.

3. The receiving organisation publishes its own ARIA Agent Trust Policy as a DNS TXT record on its domain: the minimum trust level it accepts, and its enforcement mode — monitor, warn or strict.

4. The agent arrives and DECLARES its credential and its intent.

5. The receiver EVALUATES both against the policy it published itself, verifying the signatures locally with the open-source verifier.

6. The receiver ADMITS or refuses, returning a defined response code — so a refusal is auditable and machine-readable, never a silent drop.

7. If the credential is later suspended or revoked, the event is written to an append-only ledger and reaches verifiers in about sixty seconds. The same agent knocking again is refused, at every door, without anyone being notified by hand.

useCases.title: Making the European Business Wallet real: EBW trial for national healthcare data exchange (KIK-V)
useCases.summary: Together with Zorginstituut Nederland (the Dutch National Health Care Institute), TrustTech designed, built and demonstrated a complete European Business Wallet chain for data exchange between organisations, from business identity and machine-readable mandates to qualified seals and registered, non-repudiable delivery. The context is KIK-V, the national programme for system-to-system exchange of accountability data between thousands of care providers and public bodies. Trust there was implicit, anchored in contracts and accounts rather than in the transactions. Wallets and verifiable credentials move that trust into the transaction. Organisation identification is issued as a qualified attestation (QEAA) aligned with emerging LPID/EBWOID formats, mandates prove who acts on behalf of the organisation, and employees sign in with their personal EUDI wallet. Nothing was rebuilt: the existing decentralised exchange stayed intact and every EBW capability docked onto it. The chain was demonstrated in 12 weeks and the findings adopted nationally.
useCases.userJourney:
An employee signs in to the organisation's business wallet with their personal EUDI wallet; organisational credentials belong to the company, the access pass to the person.
The organisation identifies itself with a qualified attestation (QEAA) aligned with LPID/EBWOID formats: one identity, reusable across every chain.
A machine-readable mandate credential proves the person or system acts on behalf of the organisation; differentiated per process, instantly revocable, verified at the moment of the transaction.
The submission is sealed machine-to-machine with a qualified electronic seal (QSeal, JAdES-LTA, eIDAS art. 35) via a qualified trust service provider, then delivered to the receiving public body through QERDS (ETSI TS 119 522) with a qualified timestamp.
QERDS logs evidence events for submission, acceptance and delivery in a searchable audit trail, and the receiver acknowledges receipt. Both parties hold non-repudiable proof: the sender can prove it delivered on time and unaltered, the receiver what it received, registered mail, machine-to-machine.

useCases.title: Passwordless and Verifiable Workforce Identity: Securing Ukraine’s Data Integrity
useCases.summary:
This pilot closes a gap in Ukraine's public-sector security: verifying external contractors before granting digital access. 

The State Agency for Infrastructure Restoration and Development of Ukraine already uses Hideez Development's FIDO2 passwordless authentication for internal staff, but its distributed contractors, maintaining regional surveillance and other infrastructure systems sit outside the internal domain. Creating full domain accounts or issuing passwords for them would be inefficient and risky, with no way to confirm affiliation at access time.

The project's goal is to add a verifiable credential layer from Turing Space (Netherlands) ahead of login, ties contractor authorisation to real-time organisational status via OpenID for Verifiable Credentials, and enables automatic revocation without manual admin work. Hideez calls the Turing Space Verifier API to enforce this check.

The pilot aligns with Ukrainian trust-service law, EU NIS2 Article 21, the Dutch Cyberbeveiligingswet, and eIDAS2, producing a validated, reusable model for contractor access applicable to other Ukrainian agencies and Dutch/EU organisations facing similar supply-chain risks.

useCases.title: Arattai: Verified Social Media Profiles
useCases.summary:
Arattai is an Indian instant messaging and social networking platform (Like WhatsApp and Signal) with 8 million users that enables users to connect, communicate, and build trusted online communities. By integrating with the Aadhaar App, Arattai can offer users the option to verify their identity and receive a Verified Profile badge.

Users can securely share a digitally signed verifiable credential from the Aadhaar App with their explicit consent, allowing Arattai to confirm that the profile belongs to a real individual without storing or exposing unnecessary personal information. This helps reduce fake accounts, impersonation, bots, and identity fraud while enabling users to build credibility and trust on the platform. The verification is privacy-preserving, paperless, and based on cryptographically verifiable digital credentials, giving users greater control over their identity while fostering a safer and more authentic social media experience. Arattai does 10,000 -15, 000 presentation based verification per month for their social media profiles.
useCases.userJourney:
A user downloads Arattai, creates a profile, and can immediately access the platform's messaging and social features without completing identity verification.

If the user chooses to verify their profile, Arattai initiates an app-to-app verification request to the Aadhaar App or another compatible digital identity wallet, such as Google Wallet. The user reviews the identity request and provides consent to share the required credential.

The wallet presents a verifiable identity credential to Arattai. Arattai cryptographically verifies the credential and, once verification is successful, updates the user's profile to display a verified status.

Other users can then see that the profile has been verified using a trusted digital identity credential. The verification provides an additional layer of assurance without requiring Arattai to collect or store copies of the user's identity document.

useCases.title: Urban Company: Service Professional and Customer Identity Verification
useCases.summary:
Urban Company (Think Helpling, Taskrabbit, Bark etc) is one of Asia's leading technology platforms for 8.4 million users delivering home services, connecting customers with verified professionals across categories such as beauty, wellness, home cleaning, appliance repair, plumbing, electrical services, and home improvement.

Urban Company uses the Aadhaar App to enable secure, consent-based identity verification for both service professionals and customers. Service professionals can instantly verify their identity during onboarding, periodic re-verification, or before undertaking services at customer premises. Using digitally signed verifiable credentials, the Aadhaar App enables users to share only the information necessary for the transaction, eliminating the need for physical identity documents. This reduces impersonation and fraud, streamlines onboarding and service delivery, enhances trust between professionals and customers, and provides a seamless, privacy-preserving verification experience. Urban Company has been live with Aadhaar App-based verification for the past three months and currently conducts approximately 50,000–75,000 verifications per month, with 60,590 transact
useCases.userJourney:
### How It Works

1. A service professional begins onboarding through the Urban Company Partner App.

2. As part of the onboarding journey, the Partner App initiates an identity verification request by invoking the Aadhaar App.

3. The Aadhaar App opens and prompts the professional for consent to share the required identity information.

4. Upon consent, the Aadhaar App securely retrieves the required Aadhaar-based verifiable credential from the wallet and generates a digitally signed presentation containing only the requested demographic attributes.

5. The Aadhaar App returns the signed identity response directly to the Urban Company Partner App, which verifies the credential cryptographically using UIDAI's trust framework.

6. Once verification is successful, the professional's identity is confirmed instantly, allowing the onboarding process to continue without requiring physical documents, manual data entry, or document uploads.

This seamless app-to-app interaction enables secure, privacy-preserving, and paperless onboarding while significantly reducing onboarding time and the risk of document fraud or impersonation.

useCases.title: Hala Mobility: Verified Rider Onboarding

useCases.userJourney:
How It Works

useCases.title: Swiggy: Delivery Agent and Customer Identity Verification
useCases.summary:

useCases.title: Verifiable AI fairness: a seal for the system, a receipt for the person
useCases.summary:
When an AI screens a job application, scores a loan or decides a benefit, the person affected gets a decision but often no way to verify whether it was fair or understand why. validant.ai closes this gap with two verifiable credentials.

The AI Fairness Seal is issued for the AI system. A resolver determines the appropriate fairness and explainability assessments for the jurisdiction and use case. A measurement engine calculates and cryptographically signs the results, and our server derives the verdict, so the audited party cannot assert its own outcome.

The Decision Receipt is the person’s credential, held in their wallet. It identifies the deciding system, confirms that it held a valid seal at the time, and can state what would have needed to change for a different outcome. It can be selectively presented to a third party, disclosing only what the person chooses.

The system is integrated with Switzerland’s swiyu trust infrastructure and uses SD-JWT VC, did:web and did:webvh, ES256, OpenID4VCI and OpenID4VP, with IETF Token Status List revocation. Anyone can verify a seal at validant.ai/verify without an account.

Production-ready and end-to-end validated in pre-production.
useCases.userJourney:
1. An employer runs its CV-screening AI through validant.ai, self-service or commissioned, against a named, legally grounded fairness rule.
2. The engine computes and signs the metrics (Ed25519) with the CI method, multiplicity correction and minimum detectable effect.
3. validant.ai verifies the signature and derives the verdict itself; unsigned metrics are refused. A pass is earned, not claimed.
4. The Fairness Seal is issued as an SD-JWT VC (ES256, did:web:validant.ai): system, owner, LEI, metric, threshold, result, status pointer.
5. It arrives via OpenID4VCI in the employer's wallet; swiyu confirms the issuer.
6. The AI rejects Maria; the rejection email carries the seal as a scannable code.
7. She also gets a key-bound Decision Receipt in her swiyu wallet: which system decided, that its seal was valid, the decisive factors, and the smallest change that would have flipped it.
8. She presents it selectively over OpenID4VP to an ombuds office, which re-verifies the seal.
9. Anyone can verify a seal at validant.ai/verify, no login, in-browser, public key and status list.
10. If the assessment is invalidated, the seal is revoked and every check reads Revoked within seconds.

useCases.title: Vesta Appliances: from impostors to Proof-of-Trust
useCases.summary:
Vesta Appliances is a fictional Swiss manufacturer with a very real problem: forty years of brand trust and no way to prove it online. Customers chat with fake support agents trading on Vesta's name, impostor technicians ring doorbells in Vesta livery, and nothing distinguishes the real services from the fakes.

The use case shows how Vesta becomes verifiable on the Verana Network, a public decentralized registry of registries. Its support chatbot and staff portal present ECS Service and Organization credentials as Linked Verifiable Presentations in their DID Documents, employees carry verifiable badges, repair partners hold Authorized Repairer accreditations issued under Vesta's own ecosystem governance. Anyone can resolve a Vesta service and see Proof-of-Trust before connecting: TRUSTED is earned from the credential chain, never just claimed.

It all runs live on the Verana testnet playground as an interactive story with runnable demos: verify the support chat from a personal wallet, check a technician's accreditation at the front door, and sign into the portal with a badge credential. Services are hosted by VS Agent, Verana's open-source business wallet.
useCases.userJourney:
Organization journey (Marc, CTO of Vesta): Marc deploys Vesta's Business Wallet (VS Agent) and anchors the company DID on the Verana Network. He completes KYB with an accredited issuer to obtain the ECS-Organization credential, then self-issues Service credentials so every Vesta service presents its identity as Linked VPs in its DID Document. He makes Vesta an ECS-Badge issuer for its ~200 employees and accredits a login service to verify those badges. Vesta's ISO 9001 certification becomes a verifiable credential, no re-certifying. Finally Marc builds the Vesta Repair Network, Vesta's own ecosystem with its own governance, issuing Authorized Repairer credentials that work at portal login and at the customer's front door.

User journey (runnable demos): choose a personal wallet, obtain an ECS-Badge from the demo issuer, log in to the staff portal as a repair employee with that badge instead of a password, then search the public directory of Authorized Repairers and check any repairer's Proof-of-Trust before opening the door.

useCases.title: CEXA: reusable KYC for exchanges and banks, with the original issuer paid on every reuse
useCases.summary:
Exchanges and banks run the same identity checks on the same customers, pay an IDV provider each time, and lose over half their sign-ups at the KYC wall. The Travel Rule adds a second redundancy: institutions must identify the counterparty behind every transfer, so each joins several directories and resubmits the same license.

The Crypto Exchange Association (demo) is a runnable answer built on Verana: a trust ecosystem founded by exchanges, open to the banks that serve them. It governs one reusable credential, CEXA-Kyc, on both sides: only accredited members may issue it, and only accredited members may ask a wallet for it. Asking for KYC data is a privileged, paid act. When a member accepts another member's credential, the protocol routes the reuse fee to the institution that paid for the original check: the KYC file becomes an asset, and the customer opens an account in about a minute. A second credential, CEXA-VerifiedCounterparty, published on each member's DID and free to verify, replaces N Travel Rule directory subscriptions with one membership.

The institutions are fictional. The infrastructure is not: run the full loop today with ten integrated open-source wallets.
useCases.userJourney:
1. The Association anchors its trust registry on Verana's Verifiable Public Registry: two schemas, a digest-anchored governance framework, and its fee schedule (fees are example values).

2. Members join through vetted, paid, renewable on-chain onboarding. Validated members receive their CEXA-VerifiedCounterparty credential. Members must already be Verifiable Services: the Association issues memberships, not identity.

3. The customer's first exchange runs one full IDV check, seals the evidence bundle into their wallet, digest-bound, and issues CEXA-Kyc for free.

4. On reuse, the wallet trust-resolves the requester and checks its VERIFIER accreditation before presenting. The verifier re-binds the person (passport NFC plus face match), receives the sealed evidence as its own CDD file, and pays the protocol-split fee: 0.90 to the original issuer, 0.10 to the Association. No phone home: the issuer never learns where the customer went

5. Travel Rule desks read the counterparty credential from the member's DID, free

6. Failures fail closed: a verifiable exchange outside the Association resolves TRUSTED and is still refused; a revoked credential dies at every member at the next check

useCases.title: Republic of Verandia: citizen IDs, business IDs and legal representation on one open trust registry
useCases.summary: A fictional democracy runs its own digital identity as sovereign infrastructure: every component is open source and self-hosted by its institutions, with no vendor to depend on. The Civil Registry operates its own issuing service for an eIDAS-2-compatible Citizen ID, the Business Registry issues verifiable Business IDs and Proofs of Legal Representation, and the Republic itself governs who may issue and who may verify, on a neutral public trust registry that a state can equally self-host. Citizens hold their credentials in the wallet they choose, from an open roster of independent open-source wallets, so no single app is ever mandated. One scan signs them in to the Tax Buro or their bank; an unauthorized lender's over-asking request and a fake refund portal are both refused, with proof.
useCases.userJourney: The Republic anchors everything on a Verifiable Public Registry: an open, neutral registry of ecosystems, schemas and permissions that a state can equally self-host. The National Business Registry becomes an accredited issuer of Organization credentials, so proving a company's identity is a lookup, not paperwork. The National Civil Registry runs its own open-source issuing service and creates the Citizen ID ecosystem: it defines the eIDAS-2-inspired schema and holds the ISSUER permission, while relying parties like the Tax Buro and Meridian Bank must obtain VERIFIER permissions before wallets will share anything, the registry analog of eIDAS 2 relying-party registration. Citizens scan a QR and receive the Citizen ID in any wallet from the open roster, over AnonCreds/DIDComm or OpenID4VCI (SD-JWT VC). Companies attach Business IDs to self-hosted business wallets and publish services; representatives add a Proof of Legal Representation. Before anything is shared, the wallet trust-resolves the counterparty against the registry and renders a Proof-of-Trust. An unauthorized lender that over-asks and a fake refund portal both fail resolution and are refused, with proof.

useCases.title: Agent Checkpoint: Verified Delegation for AI Agents
useCases.summary:
AI agents now act inside real people’s accounts: logging in, retrieving data, filling forms, transacting. Sites cannot tell a trusted agent from a malicious bot, so many block all automation and turn away legitimate customers. Agent traffic already runs 0.5% to 16% of customer traffic and grows monthly.

Vouched’s Agent Checkpoint ensures an agent only performs the actions its human authorized. Agent Checkpoint is built for agents: who is the human behind it, what did they permit, and an immutable audit trail proving what happened. Detect classifies agent traffic in real time. Enforce applies policy at the moment an agent acts: allow, step up authentication, or block. Govern records the delegation and consent chain.

It runs on KYA-OS, the open agent identity standard Vouched authored and donated to the Decentralized Identity Foundation with v1.0.0 in 2026.
useCases.userJourney:
A user asks an AI agent to pay an invoice. The agent calls the organisation's protected endpoint and is refused: needs_authorization, with a consent URL.

The human opens it and sees what's delegated: which agent (by DID), scope (payments.transfer), cap (10 CHEQ), 48h validity. On approval, the Responsible Party issues a W3C Verifiable Credential into the agent's wallet. The cap sits in the signed credential, not app code; a status-list entry is anchored on-chain.

The agent retries, its wallet signing a holder proof with the agent's did:key; the LLM holds no keys. The organisation verifies against the ledger: issuer DID document, status-list signature, purpose parity, expiry, holder binding, revocation bit, every call, ~0.8s. Payment executes from the organisation's own wallet, returning a detached-JWS receipt. Over-cap or stolen-credential attempts fail pre-handler.

To revoke, the human touches a FIDO2 key; the WebAuthn challenge is a hash of the revocation intent. An append-only status-list version publishes on-chain, so nobody can un-revoke quietly. Its next transfer is refused: CREDENTIAL_REVOKED.

Two wallets: the agent's credential wallet, the organisation's value wallet.
